1093.title: the Sri Sukta
1093.hook: a procession you hear before you see it: horses, a chariot, elephants, and a request that the goddess be glad to come
1093.howItsDone: In Lakshmi worship at home, some families clean the house and light lamps before reciting the Sri Sukta, especially at Diwali, as a way of welcoming the goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta asked for the Lakshmi who does not go away: a fortune that stays. Today, the hymn hears her coming.
screen: `THE ONE WHO DOES NOT GO AWAY.`

segments.voice: You hear a wedding procession before you see it. Drums from two streets over. Then horns, then a crowd, then the horse with the groom on it, swaying, decorated, a little embarrassed. Everyone on the block comes to the window. Something important is arriving, and it's loud about it. The next line of the Sri Sukta sounds like that. The singer hears the goddess coming before she's in the room. And when she gets there, he doesn't ask for anything yet. He asks one thing about her.
screen: `DRUMS FROM TWO STREETS OVER.` → `EVERYONE COMES TO THE WINDOW.` → `SOMETHING IMPORTANT ARRIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Horses go before her, a chariot carries her in the middle, and she delights in the trumpeting of elephants. I call the goddess Sri near. May the goddess Sri be pleased with me. Start with the picture: royalty arriving. Horses up front, the chariot at the center, elephants calling out. Sri comes the way a queen comes into a city, and the whole street knows. Then the verb. I call her near. The singer is still inviting, still standing at the door. And then the request, quieter than you'd expect. Not give me. Not bless me. May she be pleased with me. The Sanskrit word carries the sense of taking pleasure in, being glad of. That changes the shape of the whole hymn. It isn't a vending machine, coins in and fortune out. It's closer to hosting someone you love and hoping they feel at home. You can't order a guest to be happy. You can sweep the floor, light the lamp, and hope. Notice the name, too. Sri is the name people put in front of other names, a mark of honor on a letter, a temple sign, a wedding card. In this hymn it's the goddess herself: radiance, beauty, good fortune, all in one word. Some readers hear a little of her light in that small honor. Some hear the elephants and chariots as outer prosperity, the kind a kingdom can see; others, as the inner signs that grace is near. The hymn keeps the noise and the hope together.

segments.voice: Look around the room, or picture it, and notice what a welcome would look like here: one thing straightened, one light on. Then sit inside that welcome as if someone you love were on the way. If you pray, you can call the goddess, or God, near in your own words; if you don't, let the room and the breath be ready anyway.

1094.title: the Sri Sukta
1094.hook: a cook who eats last and keeps every plate full, and a goddess the hymn calls satisfied and satisfying
1094.howItsDone: Images of Lakshmi in homes and temples often show her seated or standing on a lotus, and the Sri Sukta's descriptions of her are chanted in front of such images during Lakshmi worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta heard her coming, horses, a chariot, elephants, and asked only that she be pleased to be here.

At a big family dinner there's often one person who eats last. She's been at the stove since noon. She notices your plate is empty before you do, and fills it, and fills the next one. And when she finally sits down, she doesn't look tired so much as content, the way someone looks when they had enough to give. The Sri Sukta has a phrase for that. Today the hymn stops calling the goddess and starts describing her, and one pair of words sits right in the middle.
screen: `SHE EATS LAST.` → `SHE FILLS EVERY PLATE.` → `CONTENT, NOT TIRED.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Smiling, within a wall of gold, moist and blazing, satisfied and satisfying, standing on the lotus, the color of the lotus: I call Sri near. A portrait painted fast, one quality after another. Start with the strange pairing: moist and blazing. Wet and on fire at once. Some readers hear the moisture as tenderness, the softness of compassion, and the blaze as her radiance. Others hear the monsoon and the sun together, the two things a field needs to grow. The hymn doesn't explain; it lets her hold both. Then the pair this day is about: satisfied, and satisfying. In Sanskrit the two words share a root sound, triptam tarpayantim, so you can hear them echo. She is full, and she makes others full. Notice the order. Her fullness comes first, and the filling flows out of it. That's the cook at the dinner table: she isn't giving from an empty pot. And then the lotus. She stands on it, and she's its color. The lotus comes back later in this hymn, and in pictures of Lakshmi you may have seen, seated or standing on that flower. Here it's simply where she is. Put the portrait together and it's not a stern queen behind a gold wall. She's smiling, soft and bright. She has enough, and so she shares. Some teachers say that's the kind of fortune the hymn is after: wealth with a face like hers, not anxious, not hoarding, glad to fill the next plate.

segments.voice: Let the breath come in all the way, without forcing it, and go out slowly, as if you're giving it away: in until you're full, out as a gift. If a face comes to mind, someone who could use a little of what you have, let them sit with you on the out-breath. If you pray, you can offer them to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, just keep breathing in and giving out.

1095.title: the Sri Sukta
1095.hook: a letter that starts 'to whom it may concern' and ends with a name: the line where the hymn stops saying 'her' and says 'you'
1095.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Sri Sukta in full during Lakshmi worship at home or in temples, so this verse of refuge is spoken as part of the whole hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta painted her portrait: smiling, moist and blazing, satisfied and satisfying.

A cover letter begins: to whom it may concern. Polite, careful, written to a title. Three paragraphs later, if the job matters enough, it starts to sound like a person talking to a person. A speech at a retirement party can go the same way: it starts about the colleague, and ends turned toward her, glass up, speaking to her directly. Something like that happens in the Sri Sukta today. For several lines the singer has talked about the goddess. Called her near. Described her. Then, at the end of one line, the pronoun changes.
screen: `TO WHOM IT MAY CONCERN.` → `A PERSON TALKING TO A PERSON.` → `THE PRONOUN CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Bright as the moon, shining, blazing with glory, Sri, cherished by the gods, generous: I take refuge in her, the lotus one. May misfortune be gone from me. I choose you. The first half is still the portrait: moonlight, glory, generosity. Then a step closer. I take refuge in her. Refuge is a strong word. It's what you look for when the weather turns, or when you've run out of ways to manage on your own. The singer isn't only admiring her now; he's placing himself under her shelter. Then the request: may misfortune be gone. The hymn's word for misfortune is Alakshmi, and she'll come back later with a face of her own. For now, she's simply what the singer wants gone. And then the last two words. Tvam vrine. I choose you. All along it's been she, her, Sri. Suddenly it's you. The singer turns and speaks to her face to face. And the verb is choose, the kind of word a person might use for choosing a partner, or a guide. Not I want your gold. I choose you. Some readers hear the heart of the whole hymn in that turn: underneath the cattle and the gold, the singer is choosing the goddess herself. Others keep the plain sense close: a person in trouble, asking for shelter and for hard luck to end. Both can be true in one breath. People in trouble still choose whom to turn to.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that's been weighing on you, a stretch of bad luck or a worry you keep circling, and let it be there. Then ask yourself, gently, where you go for shelter, a person, a place, a practice, a prayer, and turn toward it in your mind, the way the hymn turns from her to you. If you pray, you can speak to the goddess, or to God, directly; if you don't, simply rest under whatever shelter you found.

1096.title: the Sri Sukta
1096.hook: a fruit with a shell you need a hammer for, and a tree the hymn says was born from the goddess's discipline
1096.howItsDone: The bilva tree is treated as sacred in Hindu worship, where its leaves are offered, and this verse is recited as part of the Sri Sukta in Lakshmi worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta turned to her directly: I take refuge, I choose you. Today, a tree.

The bilva fruit does not look generous. It's round and greenish-gold, with a shell so hard that people crack it against a stone step or with the back of a cleaver. Inside is a sticky, fragrant pulp that some families stir into a cool summer drink. It's the same tree whose leaves this path saw offered to Shiva. You might expect a softer fruit for a goddess of abundance, a mango, maybe. But when the Sri Sukta names her tree, it names this one. And it says where the tree came from.
screen: `A SHELL YOU NEED A HAMMER FOR.` → `FRAGRANT PULP INSIDE.` → `HER TREE IS THE BILVA.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. O you who are the color of the sun, from your tapas the lord of the forest was born: your tree, the bilva. May its fruits, by tapas, drive away the misfortunes within and without. Start with tapas. It means heat, and then the heat of discipline: effort, austerity, the steady inner fire of someone who keeps at a hard practice. In the old stories, it's the fire sages keep burning in the forest. And here's the surprise: the hymn gives tapas to Sri. The goddess of fortune, gold and ease is the one whose discipline makes the tree grow. In this line, abundance isn't the opposite of effort. It comes out of it. Then the tree. Lord of the forest is an old way of saying a great tree. Its fruits have a job, to push away misfortune, and they do it by tapas too: the heat that grew the tree works through what it bears. Now, misfortunes within and without. The outer ones are easy to list: a failed harvest, an empty purse, a roof that leaks. The inner ones are harder to name. Some readers hear confusion there, illusion, the habits of mind that block a person from within. Others hear the plain sense, trouble inside the house as well as outside it. Either way, fortune isn't only something out there. And it chose a fruit you can't open without effort. Some readers find that fitting: the good thing is inside, and getting to it takes a little heat.

segments.voice: Choose to stay still, really still, for the whole sit, even when something itches or the mind wants to wander: that's tapas at its smallest, staying a little longer than is comfortable. When the mind wanders, bring it back; the bringing back is the practice. If you pray, you can offer the effort to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, let the stillness be its own offering.

1097.title: the Sri Sukta
1097.hook: a junk drawer, a sink full of dishes, and a hymn that gives misfortune a face and shows it the door
1097.howItsDone: Some Hindu households clean the house thoroughly before Diwali and Lakshmi worship, and some describe it as clearing Alakshmi out before welcoming Lakshmi in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta named her tree, the bilva, born from her own tapas. Today, the hymn meets the one it wants gone.

A home can have a corner that sags. The junk drawer that won't close. The sink that's been full since Tuesday. The pile of mail nobody wants to open. None of it is a disaster. But walk into a room like that when you're already tired, and something heavy can settle on the shoulders. The Sri Sukta has a name for that heaviness, and it isn't shy about it. A few lines ago the singer asked for misfortune to be gone. Today the hymn describes her, and then rolls up its sleeves.
screen: `THE DRAWER THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `THE SINK FULL SINCE TUESDAY.` → `A NAME FOR THE HEAVINESS.`

segments.voice: Just before this, the hymn asks for a friend of the gods to come with fame and a jewel; tradition hears Kubera there, keeper of treasure. Then the line this day is about, in paraphrase. Hunger and thirst and grime, the elder one, Alakshmi: I drive her away. Non-prosperity, lack, all of it, push it out of my house. Alakshmi is the hymn's word for misfortune, the shadow of Lakshmi. And look at what she's made of. Not curses or monsters. Hunger. Thirst. Dirt. The ordinary signs of a house that's struggling. Then the word elder. Tradition says, in later tellings, that Alakshmi is Lakshmi's older sister, and some honor her as a goddess in her own right, under the name Jyeshtha, the elder. The hymn itself just gives the word and moves on. Now the grammar, because it's the surprise. The first verb is I. I drive her away. For once, the singer isn't only asking; he takes part. Then he turns back to the goddess: you, push the rest out of my house. Some readers hear a partnership in that: the person sweeps, and grace finishes the work. Others hear the hymn's plain realism. Fortune in this hymn lives in a household, and a household has dishes and floors and a pantry to keep. Either way, misfortune here isn't a fate from the sky. It's something with a face and an address, and the singer is willing to show it the door.

1098.title: the Sri Sukta
1098.hook: a cowshed at dawn, smoke and jasmine in the same breath, and a goddess whose doorway is fragrance
1098.howItsDone: In some Hindu homes, especially in villages, cattle are honored at festivals and floors and courtyards are freshly plastered and decorated before Lakshmi worship; the Sri Sukta is chanted as part of that worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta gave misfortune a face, Alakshmi, and the singer helped show her the door.

A village before sunrise smells like several things at once. Woodsmoke. Wet earth. Milk warming in a pot. The cowshed, which nobody would call perfume. And then, from somewhere, a string of jasmine on a doorframe. Every one of those smells means the household is alive: fuel, food, animals fed, someone who cared enough to hang flowers. Today's lines of the Sri Sukta smell like that morning. The riches they name start in the cowshed and end in a person's mouth.
screen: `WOODSMOKE, WET EARTH, WARM MILK.` → `THE COWSHED, AND JASMINE.` → `A HOUSEHOLD THAT'S ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in paraphrase. Her doorway is fragrance. She is hard to overcome, always flourishing, rich in cow dung, the queen of all beings: I call Sri near. Yes, rich in cow dung. It's there in the Sanskrit, karishini, right next to queen of all beings, and the hymn sees no contradiction. In a farming household, dung is fuel for the fire, food for the fields and plaster for the floor. It means the cattle are healthy and the soil will feed you. So the goddess of fortune smells of jasmine at the door and of the cowshed out back, and both are signs of her. Now the next line, which goes somewhere else entirely. In paraphrase: may we gain the wish of the mind, the intention of the heart, the truth of speech. The beauty of cattle, and of food. May Sri and good name rest in me. First it asks for things nobody can store in a barn: the mind's wish fulfilled, an intention carried through, truth in what you say. In a hymn about fortune, truth of speech is counted as riches. Some readers hear the two lines as a pair. One is the outer household: animals, fuel, fields, a fragrant door. The other is the inner one: a clear mind, a kept intention, honest words. And the hymn asks that Sri rest in the person, not only in the barn. Others simply hear a full life, described from the ground up. Either way, the fortune this hymn wants is wider than money, and earthier, and it includes the way a person talks.

If you pray, you can give thanks to the goddess, or to God, for both; if you don't, let yourself be a little richer than you thought.

1099.title: the Sri Sukta
1099.hook: a lotus pond drained in summer, all mud, and a hymn that asks the mud itself to bring the goddess home
1099.howItsDone: Some Hindus chant the whole Sri Sukta at home or in temples during Lakshmi worship, at Diwali and on other days, often while offering lotus flowers, lamps and sweets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta counted truth of speech among its riches. Today, she's asked to stay for good, and a week ends.

Drain a lotus pond in the dry season and you don't find anything pretty. You find mud, thick and dark, with old roots running through it like cables. But that's where the flower lives. Every bloom draws on what's down there in the dark. The Sri Sukta has been calling the lotus goddess all week. And when it finally asks her to move in for good, it doesn't ask the flower to do the inviting. It asks the mud.
screen: `DRAIN THE POND. FIND MUD.` → `THAT'S WHERE THE FLOWER LIVES.` → `THE HYMN ASKS THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Through Kardama she has children. Kardama, come and dwell with me. Make Sri, the mother garlanded with lotuses, dwell in my family. Kardama is a name, and as a word it means mud. Tradition hears him as her son. So the singer asks her own child to move in, so his mother will follow. The next line does the same with water. In paraphrase: may the waters bring forth soft and gentle things. Chiklita, live in my house, and make the divine mother Sri dwell in my family. Chiklita, tradition says, is another of her children, linked to moisture. Mud and water: the two humble things a lotus can't live without. He doesn't ask the gold or the elephants to bring her, but the plainest, dampest parts of the earth. And notice the word family. Not my house only, but my line, my people. Some readers hear the ones who come after in that word, a fortune asked to stay across generations. That's this week in one picture: a procession, a goddess satisfied and satisfying, I choose you, a bilva tree, Alakshmi shown the door, cow dung and truth of speech, and now mud and water, asked to bring her home. Some readers say the lotus in the mud is the whole hymn: fortune that grows out of ordinary ground. Others keep it plain: a family praying for good seasons. The hymn goes on a little further, but this is where the path leaves it. Tomorrow, a different hymn, one that praises the goddess by her names.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something plain that holds your life up: a hard season you came through, a parent's ordinary work, the early mornings. Then notice what has grown out of it that you're glad of now, and rest with the two together, root and flower. If you pray, you can thank the goddess, or God, for both; if you don't, let the plain thing be honored for once.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn that calls Sri near, chooses her, and finally asks Kardama, the mud, to bring the lotus mother home to stay.
